edition.editorialNote: Prioritises substantial developments reported during the day, while giving space to consequential Danish reporting and fresh policy decisions. Claims and forecasts remain attributed where the reporting is uncertain or contested.

content.headline: Ukraine attack collapses a major span of Russia’s Crimea bridge
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine’s attack collapses a major span of Crimea bridge
content.standfirst: A road arch on the strategic crossing has fallen into the Kerch Strait, severing its direct road link to Russia. The railway span remains standing but is damaged, and the full effect on Russian supply routes is still uncertain.

image.caption: Footage shows a Ukrainian missile approaching the Crimean Bridge.

sources.originalTitle: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia

segments.body: Ukraine says it spent weeks weakening the bridge’s defences before a seven-stage operation involving drones and missiles. Images show a large section of the road arch collapsed into the strait; Russia says it will rebuild the crossing.

segments.title: A difficult repair and a disrupted route
segments.body: The road crossing is out of action. Trains have resumed, although the railway arch may also be damaged. An engineering consultant told the BBC that restoring full road traffic could take more than a year; the long-term repair outlook remains unclear.

The bridge is a major route for Russian forces and supplies to occupied Crimea. A land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine remains available, but ferry and sea routes have limited capacity and are vulnerable to attack. Debris may also obstruct shipping beneath the bridge.

content.headline: US loses measles elimination status after sustained spread
content.shortHeadline: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years
content.standfirst: The Pan American Health Organization says the same measles strain has circulated in the US for more than a year. More than 5,400 cases and 10 deaths have been reported this year, amid falling vaccination coverage.

sources.originalTitle: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers

segments.body: The US has lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization says, following more than 12 months of uninterrupted transmission of the same strain. Mexico and Bolivia have also lost the status, while Canada is working to interrupt transmission after losing it last year.

segments.title: Vaccination gaps
segments.body: US states have reported more than 5,400 cases this year, the highest annual total since 1991, and 10 deaths, the most since the 1990s. The national MMR vaccination rate is 92.4%, below the 95% level cited for community protection. PAHO says affected countries must submit plans to improve vaccination rates.

Public-health experts quoted by the BBC link the resurgence to vaccination gaps and declining trust, while the US health department did not respond to the BBC’s request for comment. The virus can cause serious illness; the US recommends two MMR doses for children aged one to six.

content.headline: Palestinian woman, 72, killed in West Bank shooting amid conflicting accounts
content.shortHeadline: Palestinian woman, 72, killed in West Bank shooting
content.standfirst: The Palestinian health ministry says Fadda al-Fahidat was shot dead in a village near Jericho. Local Palestinians and the Israeli military give conflicting accounts of the events that led to the shooting.

image.caption: A funeral was held for Fadda al-Fahidat in al-Duyuk al-Tahta.

sources.originalTitle: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says

segments.body: Fadda al-Fahidat, 72, was shot in the head and died in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, according to Palestinian health officials and doctors in Jericho. Local Palestinians say settlers opened fire after harassment and stone-throwing. The Israeli military says Palestinians rammed a vehicle and threw rocks, prompting settlers to fire.

segments.title: Tensions around a new outpost
segments.body: The village has been tense since settlers moved into eight houses there on 4 November. B’Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in the area; the Israeli military says its forces are pursuing suspects in the shooting.

The report also describes separate violence near Bethlehem, where Palestinians were injured by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler, according to Palestinian officials; the Israeli military called that incident a traffic accident. These accounts have not been independently resolved in the supplied reporting.

content.headline: US expands scrutiny of chip computing in South-East Asia and Brazil
content.shortHeadline: US tightens scrutiny of chip access in South-East Asia and Brazil
content.standfirst: New US rules require licences for some data-centre operators to buy advanced chips or provide their computing power to Chinese firms. The measures could disrupt a route China uses to train AI models, while also affecting regional investment.

sources.originalTitle: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China

segments.body: Washington’s interim rules put data-centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil under greater scrutiny. They cover not only exports of advanced chips but access to computing power from those chips, which Chinese companies have rented abroad for artificial-intelligence work.

segments.title: A risk to regional investment
segments.body: The US Commerce Department says the countries pose a higher-than-normal risk of chip diversion. The BBC reports that firms in Malaysia and Thailand, where data-centre growth has been driven partly by Chinese buyers, could feel the impact most. One analyst says investment tied to identifiable customers and major technology companies should be more resilient.

China’s foreign ministry called the measures “economic coercion” and said Beijing would protect its interests. The rules arrive ahead of Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping. They could also strengthen pressure on Chinese companies to develop domestic chips, a longer-term trade-off for Washington.

content.headline: Trump arrives in Manila before planned talks with Xi and Putin
content.shortHeadline: Trump arrives in Asia ahead of planned Xi-Putin talks
content.standfirst: The US president began his Asian trip in the Philippines before travelling to China for a summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Trump said he would be open to meeting Putin one-to-one if the opportunity arose.

sources.originalTitle: Trump lands in Asia ahead of talks with Russian and Chinese presidents

segments.body: Donald Trump arrived in Manila for the first stop of a trip that is due to culminate in China, where he is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Asked about a separate meeting with Putin, Trump said: “If it’s available, I would.”

segments.title: Regional competition
segments.body: In Manila, Trump met leaders from the Quad—India, Japan and Australia—and described the countries as partners in a stable Indo-Pacific. The BBC reports that Washington wants regional countries to join its technology and AI ecosystem, while China’s economic influence in South-East Asia remains substantial.

content.headline: Fossil-fuel exports put Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia atop historic CO₂ tab
content.shortHeadline: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia top fossil-export emissions tally
content.standfirst: A new analysis assigns emissions to the countries that extracted and exported the fuels, rather than where they were burned. Its findings sharpen debate at COP31, where a draft text calls for a transition away from fossil fuels.

image.caption: An oil well and drilling rig at the Yarakta Oil Field in Russia.

sources.originalTitle: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia named as biggest CO2 exporters in history

segments.body: An analysis by Carbon Brief estimates that exported fossil fuels from Russia account for more than 70 gigatonnes of CO₂ through 2025, followed by about 60 gigatonnes from Saudi Arabia and more than 25 gigatonnes from Australia. The approach counts emissions where the fuels were extracted, unlike most tallies based on where they are burned.

segments.title: A debate over responsibility
segments.body: The analysis does not put the US and China below these exporters in total historical responsibility: both countries have also burned large quantities of their own fossil fuels, as well as importing them. Saudi Arabia argues that the countries consuming its oil decide how it is used and should bear responsibility for the resulting emissions.

The report comes as Australia presides over COP31. A draft summit text calls for an “immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, but negotiations remain divided and the wording may change. Separate analysis cited by the Guardian says Australia has approved coalmines expected to operate until 2088.

content.headline: Government backs Milburn’s plan to overhaul support for young people
content.shortHeadline: Government backs Milburn plan to overhaul youth employment support
content.standfirst: Ministers have endorsed the broad direction of a plan to get more young people into work, education or training, and named Alan Milburn to oversee its implementation. The proposals include more support but also tighter benefit eligibility for some under-25s.

image.caption: Young people with learning disabilities or autism take part in Project Search, a work-placement programme in east London.

sources.originalTitle: Ministers vow to create new welfare system for young people as they back Milburn report
Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?
PIP and UC health cut for under-25s: All the benefits changes in the Milburn review
UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6% as government releases Milburn report
‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
I have ADHD and autism – disgusting benefit cuts won’t help young people work
My month on universal credit with disabled sons – there’s no money left over

segments.body: The government says it wants a new system for young people after backing the recommendations in Alan Milburn’s review. Milburn will chair a new youth opportunities unit, and ministers say they will begin looking for departmental savings to help fund the proposals. A full government response is still to come.

segments.title: Support and proposed benefit changes
segments.body: Milburn proposes a youth opportunity service offering advice and a guaranteed route into education, training or work for 18- to 24-year-olds. The plan also includes more vocational courses, apprenticeships and employer incentives. It would replace some existing disability and sickness benefits for under-25s with a youth allowance and more targeted support for additional costs.

segments.title: Questions over jobs and disability support
segments.body: The report aims to reduce the share of young people not in work, education or training over a decade. Separate official figures put UK unemployment at 4.6% in September, but vacancies fell to 690,000 in October. Disability advocates and young people interviewed by the BBC and Guardian warn that reducing benefits could leave some people without support they need to work; one supported-employment programme reported that 68% of its students found jobs at the end of the course.

content.headline: Met apologises after BBC investigation into predatory rape-unit detective
content.shortHeadline: Met apologises over detective who exploited women he was meant to help
content.standfirst: A BBC investigation says the Metropolitan Police repeatedly missed chances to stop Warren Arter, who used his role investigating sexual assaults to target women. The force says it is reviewing his devices and is urging potential victims to come forward.

image.caption: BBC Panorama examines the conduct of former Metropolitan Police detective Warren Arter.

sources.originalTitle: How Met failed to stop rape-unit detective who abused women

segments.body: The BBC reports that Warren Arter exploited women whose cases he investigated while leading a south-east London sexual-assault unit. Two women told Panorama he groomed them; one says he raped her. Arter died in prison in 2024, days after his arrest on sexual-offence allegations, which were not tested at trial.

segments.title: Missed chances and unanswered questions
segments.body: The investigation found that a police watchdog had identified 21 potential victims by 2020, and that the Met had not contacted every woman whose case Arter handled. A former investigator says senior officers restricted plans to widen the inquiry; those officers dispute that account. The Met says human error delayed an arrest after an image allegation was reported in 2024.

The Metropolitan Police has publicly apologised to the women and says it is prioritising analysis of Arter’s electronic devices and examining whether there may be more victims. A former victims’ commissioner is calling for an outside force to review all the cases he handled. The Met says it is deeply sorry for the harm caused.

content.headline: UK sanctions eight firms over Israeli settlement activity in West Bank
content.shortHeadline: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
content.standfirst: The first sanctions in the government’s tougher approach target eight construction and property businesses, as well as an activist group accused of blocking aid to Gaza. The move comes before bids are due for a contested settlement project east of Jerusalem.

image.caption: The E1 area east of Jerusalem, a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank.

sources.originalTitle: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank

segments.body: The UK has sanctioned eight construction and property firms it says are involved in building Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. It has also targeted Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement the government says organised blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza. Israel has not commented on this package; it has previously condemned UK measures over settlements.

segments.title: Focus on the E1 area
segments.body: The sanctions were announced two days before bids were due for construction tenders in the E1 area east of Jerusalem. The UK government says development there would undermine the possibility of a two-state solution. The Guardian reports that the sanctions are intended to disrupt finance, though it is not yet clear how dependent the targeted firms are on British funding.

The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the move. The UK says it is also developing separate legislation to restrict imports of goods from settlements and some services connected with settlement properties; those measures are not part of the sanctions announced today.

content.headline: Asylum seekers on final UK-France return flight say they fear smugglers
content.shortHeadline: Asylum seekers on UK-France flight say return puts them at risk
content.standfirst: Some passengers on Tuesday’s final flight under the “one in, one out” pilot say they returned to the UK after being sent to France because of threats from smugglers. The Home Office says the scheme demonstrated that people returned to the UK would be sent back.

image.caption: The UK-France pilot returned some people who arrived in the UK by small boat to France.

sources.originalTitle: Asylum seekers on final ‘one in, one out’ UK-France flight feel they are being ‘punished’

segments.body: Asylum seekers due to be returned to France told the Guardian they had previously been sent there and came back to the UK after threats from smugglers. One man, who says he is an Iranian political dissident, fears being caught again and says he struggled to obtain legal advice before his removal.

segments.title: Dispute over the pilot’s impact
segments.body: The pilot exchanged some people who crossed the Channel in small boats for an equivalent number brought from northern France to claim asylum in the UK. Medical Justice called it a “disaster”. The Home Office says it successfully demonstrated that returns under such an arrangement can work; an inspector said it was unclear how the department would measure success or failure.

The scheme ended on 1 October, according to the report. Government figures cited by the Guardian show that 4,786 people crossed the Channel in 69 small boats after it ended. The Home Office says it is taking lessons from the pilot into wider work on returns.

content.headline: UK changes modern-slavery guidance to include financial exploitation
content.shortHeadline: Financially exploited migrant workers can be considered modern-slavery
content.standfirst: The Home Office has agreed to recognise financial exploitation as a possible form of modern slavery after a care worker challenged an initial refusal of his case. The change does not itself determine whether any individual qualifies for support.

sources.originalTitle: Scammed migrant workers in UK to be considered possible victims of modern slavery

segments.body: A care worker from Pakistan said he paid £22,000 for a job in the UK that did not exist, leaving him and his family in debt and without work. After he was initially found not to qualify as a potential victim of modern slavery, he challenged the decision with support from charities and legal centres.

segments.title: A change in the Home Office approach
segments.body: The Home Office admitted in a court order that it had taken an “unduly narrow approach” to exploitation. It will now recognise financial exploitation as a possible form of modern slavery and trafficking when considering cases. The worker’s case was referred back for consideration; the policy change is not an automatic ruling on every case.

The Work Rights Centre says it has encountered other cases of financial exploitation among migrant care workers. In a survey of more than 100 workers, nearly three-quarters said they had experienced some form of it. The Home Office says financial exploitation is unacceptable and that it works with enforcement and safeguarding partners where abuse is identified.

content.headline: Chloe Moffat’s parents urge employers to adopt new HR safeguards
content.shortHeadline: Parents launch HR policy after Treasury worker’s death
content.standfirst: The parents of Chloe Moffat, whose inquest found the Treasury materially contributed to her death, have launched guidance urging employers to make disciplinary processes clearer and more humane. The Treasury says it has introduced safeguards following the case.

image.caption: Chloe Moffat worked as a personal assistant at the Treasury for almost three years.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Chloe’s policy’ aims to prevent repeat of case of Treasury worker who took her own life

segments.body: Chloe Moffat, a 26-year-old Treasury employee, died by suicide the day after a surprise disciplinary meeting about allegations she denied. A coroner found the department had “materially contributed” to her death. Her parents have worked with the Global Kindness Institute to develop “Chloe’s policy” for employers.

segments.title: What the proposed guidance says
segments.body: The policy asks HR teams to consider the potential harm of disciplinary procedures, especially where allegations are anonymous or unverified; prioritise psychological safety; consider alternatives; and give staff clear information, including whether their job is at risk. Moffat’s parents want organisations to help develop and adopt it.

The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s report committed to safeguards. The report says staff should receive proper notice and be allowed a supporter at disciplinary meetings, and should be told if dismissal is not likely. Moffat’s parents say they felt listened to in a recent meeting with the department.

content.headline: Police-force merger plans could raise bills in 19 areas, analysis suggests
content.shortHeadline: Police merger proposals could raise council tax in 19 areas
content.standfirst: A report on possible police “superforces” suggests some Band D households could pay up to £70 more a year if local charges were aligned. The proposals are not final, and the Home Office says it does not recognise the speculative figures.

image.caption: A police community support officer in Newcastle, in the Northumbria force area.

sources.originalTitle: The 19 areas where council tax bills could rise by up to £70 under police reform plans

segments.body: Ministers are considering reducing England and Wales’s 43 police forces to as few as nine, though no decision has been made. An analysis by the i Paper estimates that aligning council-tax police charges across new regions could raise bills in 19 force areas and lower them in 18 others.

segments.title: Possible costs and objections
segments.body: The analysis estimates that a Band D household in Northumbria could pay £70 more a year, while bills in Surrey could fall by £53. Police and crime commissioners warn that regional forces could weaken local accountability and leave some communities paying more for a less local service.

The police precept makes up about 34% of force funding, but varies between local authorities. The Home Office says it is still reviewing recommendations on police structures and calls the figures speculative.

content.headline: Ikea abandons some UK store plans, citing business taxes
content.shortHeadline: Ikea scraps some planned UK stores over business costs
content.standfirst: Ikea says the cost and complexity of doing business in the UK led it to abandon some planned smaller stores. UK sales rose just 0.5% in the year to August as shoppers cut back on larger purchases.

image.caption: Ikea UK sales rose 0.5% to £2.26bn in the year to August.

sources.originalTitle: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes

segments.body: Ikea’s UK boss says the retailer has abandoned plans for some smaller stores because of business taxes and market complexity. The company declined to identify the locations. It says its UK operation pays more business taxes than any of its European operations.

UK sales rose 0.5% to £2.26bn in the year to the end of August. Ikea says household budget pressure and weak consumer confidence have led some shoppers to buy smaller items instead of replacing entire rooms of furniture. The company has cut prices on 425 products by an average of 20%.

content.headline: Danish authorities urge critical systems to prepare for quantum-computing threat
content.shortHeadline: Denmark sets 2029 deadline to secure critical systems from quantum
content.standfirst: New guidance from Denmark’s defence intelligence service and civil-contingencies agency says critical systems should be protected against quantum computers by the end of 2029. The agencies warn the technology could threaten some encryption sooner than previously expected.

sources.originalTitle: Myndigheder advarer mod ny cybertrussel

segments.body: Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service and Agency for Social Security and Preparedness say authorities and businesses should secure their most critical systems against quantum-computing risks by the end of 2029. Their guidance calls for organisations to map critical systems and plan a move to quantum-resistant cryptography.

segments.title: A changing estimate
segments.body: A KPMG expert quoted by TV 2 says the threat had previously been expected around 2035, but that developments in artificial intelligence have accelerated work on correcting errors in quantum computers. The new guidance warns that a sufficiently capable quantum computer could undermine some encryption used for digital signatures and identity systems, including MitID.

The agencies say the transition requires time and planning and encourage high-priority systems to move first. The article describes a future risk, not a current ability to break the protections in use today. The agencies did not comment to TV 2.

content.headline: Danish prosecutors charge 23-year-old with terrorism over alleged arson
content.shortHeadline: 23-year-old charged with terrorism over alleged Copenhagen arson
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege the man scouted addresses in the Copenhagen area and set fire to a property where residents, including a Jewish woman, were present. He is due to stand trial at Copenhagen City Court on 23 November.

sources.originalTitle: 23-årig mand tiltalt for terrorisme

segments.body: A 23-year-old man has been charged under Denmark’s terrorism law. Prosecutors allege that, between early April and 29 May 2024, he scouted addresses in the Copenhagen area where Jewish people lived, then set fire to a property while residents were inside.

The prosecution says the residents were exposed to imminent danger and will seek a prison sentence, loss of Danish citizenship and permanent expulsion from Denmark. These are allegations; the case is scheduled to be heard by a jury at Copenhagen City Court beginning on 23 November.

content.headline: Danish financial intelligence unit estimates money laundering at DKK 90bn a year
content.shortHeadline: Danish unit estimates DKK 90bn laundered annually
content.standfirst: A new estimate from Denmark’s financial intelligence unit puts annual money laundering at about DKK 90bn, much of it linked to tax and VAT fraud and drug crime. The unit says the figure is uncertain and far higher than the sums reported to authorities.

sources.originalTitle: Hvidvask-rapport: Hvert år hvidvaskes 90 milliarder kroner i Danmark

segments.body: Hvidvasksekretariatet, Denmark’s financial intelligence unit, estimates that about DKK 90bn is laundered in the country each year, according to a report cited by the National Special Crime Unit. The estimate uses a UN methodology and includes an additional amount for tax crime.

segments.title: A substantial unknown amount
segments.body: The unit says it received reports concerning an average of DKK 50bn a year over the past decade, indicating that some activity is not detected by authorities. It estimates the total at around 2.7% of GDP but stresses that the figure is uncertain.

The report says criminals are increasingly using Danish companies, potentially exposing lawyers, accountants, estate agents and other advisers to misuse. The unit says it will also produce reports on money laundering in Greenland and the Faroe Islands.

content.headline: Greenlanders born outside marriage seek compensation from Danish state
content.shortHeadline: 26 Greenlanders seek compensation over legal fatherlessness
content.standfirst: Twenty-six people born in Greenland outside marriage before 1974 are seeking DKK 150,000 each from the Danish state. They say they were denied the right to know or inherit from their fathers; the state has not settled the case, now being heard in the Eastern High Court.

image.caption: The case by 26 Greenlanders seeking compensation from the Danish state began in the Eastern High Court.

sources.originalTitle: 'Mørkt kapitel' i historien mellem Danmark og Grønland er nået til Østre Landsret: 'Fint at få ryddet op i fortidens synder'

segments.body: The case brought by 26 Greenlanders against the Danish state began in the Eastern High Court. Born outside marriage in Greenland before 1974, they say they were unable to learn who their fathers were, inherit from them or take their surnames. Each claimant seeks DKK 150,000 in compensation.

segments.title: Calls for an answer
segments.body: The state has not reached a settlement, unlike in the separate case concerning the forced contraception of Greenlandic women, for which the state has apologised and compensation has been provided. The current hearing is scheduled to run through Thursday.

A Greenland-based regional official quoted by DR says it is time to address past wrongs. A journalist cited in the report says the decision to proceed with a court case while the government considers an apology has caused confusion in Greenland.

content.headline: Rajen Shah denies charges as testimony continues in Danish tax-fraud trial
content.shortHeadline: Rajen Shah denies charges in Danish dividend-tax fraud trial
content.standfirst: A former tax expert has begun giving evidence in the trial over alleged dividend-tax fraud against the Danish state. Rajen Shah is accused of taking part in a scheme involving hundreds of millions of kroner; he denies wrongdoing.

image.caption: Rajen Shah, who denies the charges, is pictured in connection with the trial.

sources.originalTitle: Han startede på en løn på en halv million kroner. Nu er han tiltalt i danmarkshistoriens største bedragerisag

segments.body: Rajen Shah, a former tax expert at Solo Capital, is accused of fraudulently claiming DKK 300m in dividend-tax refunds between 2013 and 2015. He told the court he was among the investment firm’s early employees and described his work alongside founder Sanjay Shah, who has been convicted in a separate case and has appealed.

segments.title: What the prosecution alleges
segments.body: Prosecutors say the wider scheme used American pension funds and documents created through control of a small German bank to claim refunds on fictitious share trades. Rajen Shah confirmed making changes to a spreadsheet shown in court, but said it recorded what had happened and what could be improved. All four defendants in this trial deny the charges.
The case concerns alleged fraud against Denmark’s tax authority. Shah’s testimony is continuing at later hearings, and DR reports that a verdict is not expected until next year.

content.headline: Denmark’s car and commuting tax changes will shift costs for drivers
content.shortHeadline: Danish drivers face higher car fees and a lower commuting deduction
content.standfirst: A temporary boost to the commuting deduction will end in 2027, while vehicle ownership fees will rise for many drivers. The changes accompany a temporary cut in fuel tax, so the overall effect will vary by vehicle and travel distance.

sources.originalTitle: 1,6 millioner bilister skal betale ekstra for at eje deres bil næste år
Skatterådet: Så meget falder kørselsfradraget til næste år
Pendleres kørselsfradrag står til at falde næste år

segments.body: More than 1.6 million Danish drivers will face higher vehicle ownership fees next year, according to FDM. Some older, fuel-efficient diesel cars will incur an extra DKK 1,300 a year; many electric cars, plug-in hybrids and some petrol cars will pay DKK 380 more.

segments.title: Commuting deductions also fall from this year’s temporary level
segments.body: For commuters travelling 25 to 120 kilometres a day, the 2027 deduction rate will be DKK 2.44 per kilometre, down from this year’s temporarily raised DKK 3.17. It is still above the DKK 2.28 rate set before that temporary increase. A commuter travelling 100 kilometres a day could receive about DKK 2,800 less through the deduction, according to an analyst cited by DR.

The government’s agreement also temporarily reduces petrol and diesel taxes, with prices at the pump expected to fall by about DKK 2 per litre. FDM says the saving may be partly offset for some drivers by higher ownership fees and the lower commuting deduction; the balance depends on individual circumstances.

content.headline: UN rights chief voices concern over five-country Rwanda migration plan
content.shortHeadline: UN rights chief warns of risks in Rwanda return-centre plan
content.standfirst: Volker Türk says a proposed facility in Rwanda for people whose right to stay in Europe has ended raises human-rights concerns. Denmark and four other European countries are pursuing the plan.

image.caption: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.

sources.originalTitle: FN's menneskerettighedschef betænkelig ved Rwanda-plan

segments.body: The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, says he is concerned about human-rights risks in a plan by Denmark, Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands to establish a return centre in Rwanda. The report attributes his comments to Reuters.

Türk said the proposed destination is a country with which the people concerned have no real connection and which faces its own human-rights challenges. He called instead for a comprehensive approach to migration grounded in human rights.

content.headline: Publisher says changes to book on 112-year-old depend on her participation
content.shortHeadline: Publisher says book changes depend on Kirsten Schwalbe’s participation
content.standfirst: Gyldendal says it will revise its biography of Kirsten Schwalbe only if she takes part, after new reporting said she held a leadership role in Denmark’s Nazi party during the occupation. TV Midtvest has stopped its coverage, citing concern for her health.

image.caption: Kirsten Schwalbe’s family says recent media coverage has affected her health.

sources.originalTitle: Gyldendal ændrer kun i bog om 112-årig, hvis hun selv deltager
TV Midtvest dropper dækning af landets ældste person

segments.body: Gyldendal now says changes to its book about 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe will be made only if she participates. The publisher had earlier said it planned to add material after reporting about her wartime membership of the Danish Nazi party; further reporting cited archival documents suggesting she held a local leadership role.

segments.title: Coverage and the family’s concerns
segments.body: TV Midtvest, whose journalists wrote the book and had followed Schwalbe, has stopped further interviews and filming after her family said recent media attention had affected her health. Gyldendal says it wants to investigate the new information and consult experts before deciding what to do with the book.

content.headline: Life Without Buildings reunite, wary of spoiling the joy
content.shortHeadline: Life Without Buildings reunite, wary of spoiling the joy
content.standfirst: The Scottish quartet are back for four shows, decades after their brief, acclaimed run. They explain how Frank Ocean and TikTok helped new listeners find their music—and why returning to the stage felt both thrilling and risky.

image.caption: Life Without Buildings pictured around the release of their debut album.

sources.originalTitle: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?

segments.body: Life Without Buildings split in 2002 after three years, one studio album and modest cult success. Now the Glasgow band are playing four shows for Rough Trade’s 50th birthday. Their members had feared a reunion might diminish a joyful, self-contained moment in their past.

segments.title: A song finds a second life
segments.body: The Leanover found new listeners after Frank Ocean played it on his Apple Music show in 2018, then Beabadoobee’s TikTok brought its distinctive opening seconds to a new audience. Singer Sue Tompkins’s rhythmic, carefully scripted spoken-sung vocals remain at the centre of the band’s unusual sound.

content.headline: UK music industry revenues hit £8.4bn as working artists face pressure
content.shortHeadline: UK music hits record revenues, but working artists feel the squeeze
content.standfirst: Tours and hit albums helped music add a record £8.4bn to the UK economy in 2025. But the industry report points to rising costs for grassroots acts and a sharp gap between earnings measures for established artists and music creators.

image.caption: Noel and Liam Gallagher, whose 2025 tour helped boost music revenues.

sources.originalTitle: UK music industry hits record high of £8.4bn – but are working musicians being left behind?

segments.body: UK Music’s annual report says the industry contributed £8.4bn to the economy in 2025, up 5.7% on the previous year, while export revenue reached £4.8bn. Recorded employment rose by 730 jobs to 220,500. Major tours and successful albums helped drive the growth.

segments.title: Uneven gains
segments.body: The report warns that rising costs are reducing net income for many emerging and grassroots artists. Its survey of top- and mid-level artists found earnings up more than 14% year on year; a separate self-reported survey of music creators found growth of just 0.2%. UK Music also flags AI deepfakes as a growing problem.

content.headline: Robert Christgau’s caustic genius gets a candid documentary portrait
content.shortHeadline: The caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
content.standfirst: A new documentary follows the veteran Village Voice critic, whose sharp grades, memorable put-downs and demanding editing shaped generations of writers. Its director also explores the partnership and private life behind his long-running work.

image.caption: Robert Christgau in a still from The Last Critic.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau

segments.body: The Last Critic portrays Robert Christgau, the 84-year-old critic known for his Consumer Guide album grades and decades at the Village Voice. The film’s director, Matty Wishnow, describes a writer still listening, editing and publishing—and a career he sees as both unprecedented and difficult to repeat.

segments.title: Beyond the takedowns
segments.body: Christgau’s biting lines made him famous, but the documentary also looks at his work as an editor and his relationship with critic, novelist and editor Carola Dibbell. Wishnow argues that Christgau’s capsule reviews combine close listening with politics and cultural analysis; the film is playing at Doc NYC, with a wider release yet to be announced.

content.headline: Kadiatu Kanneh-Mason warns music education is slipping from Nottingham
content.shortHeadline: Kanneh-Mason warns of a widening gap in music education
content.standfirst: The University of Nottingham is closing its music department after a century, while school music provision faces cuts. Kadiatu Kanneh-Mason says the loss threatens opportunities for young musicians and the region’s cultural life.

image.caption: Cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason, whose musical education included support from the University of Nottingham.

sources.originalTitle: Mother of renowned musicians ‘devastated’ by closure of department at Nottingham University

segments.body: Kadiatu Kanneh-Mason says she is devastated by the University of Nottingham’s decision to close its music department, which has provided tuition for 100 years. Her children, including cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason, benefited from the university’s teachers, accompanists and performance opportunities.

segments.title: A wider concern
segments.body: Kanneh-Mason links the closure to cuts in school arts provision and a decline in A-level music participation, warning that access to musical education is becoming harder for state-school pupils. The university says changing student demand, course costs and competition informed its decision; the Department for Education says it is changing the curriculum and supporting arts access.

content.headline: Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours took shape amid rows, walk-outs and sudden inspiration
content.shortHeadline: Two turbulent days behind Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours
content.standfirst: Co-producer Ken Caillat recalls studio arguments that gave way to the vocal on “You Make Loving Fun” and the first capture of “Songbird”. He also describes how the band reshaped “The Chain” from its earlier form.

image.caption: Stevie Nicks of Fleetwood Mac, whose album Rumours included “Dreams”.

sources.originalTitle: Two explosive days in the making of Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours

segments.body: Ken Caillat recalls recording Rumours as a tense and unpredictable process. During one session, Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham argued between takes, then returned to the microphones and recorded their parts for “You Make Loving Fun”. The conflict did not stop the music from moving forward.

segments.title: Songs discovered and rebuilt
segments.body: Caillat says he captured Christine McVie playing “Songbird” at the piano after the band had left the room, then proposed recording it at Berkeley Community Theater. He also describes rebuilding “The Chain” around Mick Fleetwood’s kick-drum part and Buckingham’s Dobro before the band developed the song further.

content.headline: Snoh Aalegra reaches for Prince’s Minneapolis sound on Legendary Love
content.shortHeadline: Snoh Aalegra’s ambitious, yearning Legendary Love
content.standfirst: The Swedish-Iranian singer draws directly on the Minneapolis sound with analog synths, drum machines and contributions from Jimmy Jam, Terry Lewis and Nile Rodgers. The review finds her most ambitious album yet, though some of its polish blunts the emotion.

sources.originalTitle: Legendary Love

segments.body: On Legendary Love, Snoh Aalegra channels the Minneapolis sound associated with her mentor Prince. The Swedish-Iranian singer works with analog synths and drum machines, and brings in producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis for an album built around longing and uncertain romance.

segments.title: Gloss and feeling
segments.body: The review praises Aalegra’s vocal control and the arrangements on songs including “I Love You” and “Warmest Shade of Blue”. It also finds the production too clean on some tracks, leaving the heartbreak at a distance. The verdict: a heartfelt and expertly made album, with room for a more singular emotional release.

content.headline: Cute turn apocalyptic noise into a portrait of a world under strain
content.shortHeadline: Cute’s apocalyptic debut finds a path through the noise
content.standfirst: The Canadian quartet’s first album pares their sprawling sludgegaze into five long, escalating tracks. The review hears both the psychological turmoil of its subjects and a fragile suggestion of endurance.

sources.originalTitle: history is not woven by innocent hands

segments.body: Hamilton, Ontario band cute play in darkness, facing one another under headlamps. Their debut album, history is not woven by innocent hands, turns that stark live approach into five extended tracks that move from post-hardcore tension to towering noise and post-rock scale.

segments.title: Noise as narrative
segments.body: The review describes songs that build tension rather than rely on simple quiet-to-loud shocks. “Room full of mirrors” follows a family man confronting a home invasion, while “force majeure” shifts into a more personal confession. The album’s harshness reflects a punishing world, but the closing refrain leaves open the possibility of facing another day.

content.headline: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders turns everyday scenes into political art
content.shortHeadline: Armand Hammer make language—and politics—on Snakes & Ladders
content.standfirst: billy woods and Elucid build their latest album around intricate writing and a wide-ranging circle of independent producers. The review hears a demanding, timely record that finds political meaning in daily life.

sources.originalTitle: Snakes & Ladders

segments.body: The New York duo Armand Hammer, formed by billy woods and Elucid, surprise-released Snakes & Ladders on Backwoodz Studioz. The album pairs their fragmented, sharply observed verses with production from collaborators including clipping., Preservation, Kenny Segal and Child Actor.

segments.title: A record for anxious times
segments.body: The review finds the album’s political force in its attention to ordinary places and experiences, from a walk along Bushwick Avenue to the intrusion of AI in a job application. It argues that Armand Hammer’s work matters beyond commercial measures, while acknowledging that the record is deliberately difficult to parse.

content.headline: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping review – a weary prequel
content.shortHeadline: Sunrise on the Reaping is a weary Hunger Games prequel
content.standfirst: The latest return to Panem follows a young Haymitch Abernathy, but the review finds its characters unconvincing and its familiar dystopia drained of purpose. It argues the film has little reason to exist beyond extending the franchise.

image.caption: Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

sources.originalTitle: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping review – surreally awful prequel to the Katniss Everdeen era

segments.body: Sunrise on the Reaping returns to the Hunger Games world before Katniss Everdeen’s story. Joseph Zada plays the teenage Haymitch Abernathy, who is selected for the televised death match and draws the attention of President Snow, played by Ralph Fiennes.

segments.title: A franchise running on fumes
segments.body: The review criticises the film’s pantomime-like ruling class and says its grim depiction of ordinary life sits awkwardly beside those characters. It also questions the story’s dramatic logic, arguing that the prequel neither explains the Games’ origins nor offers an authentic reason to revisit the franchise.

content.headline: American Doctor follows US medics working amid devastation in Gaza
content.shortHeadline: American Doctor follows medics risking their lives in Gaza
content.standfirst: Poh Si Teng’s documentary follows three American doctors who volunteer at Nasser hospital in early 2025. The review describes the hospital’s mass-casualty work and the doctors’ efforts to speak publicly about what they witnessed.

image.caption: Dr Mark Perlmutter in American Doctor.

sources.originalTitle: American Doctor review – medics put their lives on the line in Gaza amid the carnage

segments.body: American Doctor follows three US doctors who volunteer at Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025. Thaer Ahmad, a Palestinian American emergency doctor, is refused entry; trauma surgeon Feroze Sidhwa and orthopaedic surgeon Mark Perlmutter make the journey.

segments.title: Witnessing the hospital’s work
segments.body: The review describes camaraderie among medical staff and the strain of treating mass casualties without always having pain medicine. It says the film also follows the doctors as they advocate for Palestine after returning to the US. The gathered review reports that a Palestinian surgeon featured in the film, Rizk Abu Shaira, was killed in a recent airstrike.

content.headline: Rocky became Philadelphia’s founding myth—and 50 years later it endures
content.shortHeadline: Rocky remains Philadelphia’s underdog myth, 50 years on
content.standfirst: A new film about Sylvester Stallone’s fight to make Rocky renews the story of an underdog who became a city symbol. The anniversary invites a harder look at whose lives become universal in Philadelphia’s self-image.

image.caption: Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa.

sources.originalTitle: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it

segments.body: Fifty years after its release, Rocky remains deeply woven into Philadelphia’s public identity. A new film, I Play Rocky, retells Sylvester Stallone’s struggle to get his script made and play the unknown boxer himself—an underdog story that mirrors the character’s fight for a chance.

segments.title: The myth and the city
segments.body: The essay argues that Rocky’s appeal has outlasted the original film through sequels and generations of stories built on the same underdog template. It also contrasts the fictional, white Italian American boxer’s prominence with the lesser-known legacy of real Black champion Joe Frazier, asking whose experiences a city turns into universal myths.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson is James Bond: the casting is only the beginning
content.shortHeadline: Pattinson’s Bond casting begins a long road to Bond 26
content.standfirst: The new 007 has been chosen, but the script, supporting cast, production timetable and marketing remain unresolved. A second analysis questions whether an established franchise star can bring Bond the fresh start the role has often offered.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson, cast as the next James Bond.

sources.originalTitle: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. So what happens next?
The big problem with Robert Pattinson playing Bond

segments.body: Robert Pattinson has been cast as James Bond in the 26th official film. The project’s writer, Steven Knight, has delivered a first draft, but the film’s release date, title, full cast and production schedule remain unsettled. Industry rumours cited by the Guardian point to production in 2027 and a possible November 2028 release.

segments.title: What the role asks of its star
segments.body: The next challenge is balancing Bond’s established conventions with contemporary expectations, then turning the film into a global event. The i Paper’s analysis argues that Pattinson’s fame and franchise experience may make it harder for him to disappear into the part, while warning that the role could constrain an actor known for moving between blockbuster and arthouse work.

perspectives.body: The i Paper frames the casting as a break with Bond tradition: earlier actors were less established when chosen, while Pattinson already carries a prominent franchise history. It sees that as a potential obstacle to reinvention, not a prediction of failure.

content.headline: Heysel 85 review – a furious account of the football disaster
content.shortHeadline: Heysel 85 indicts the failures behind a football disaster
content.standfirst: Teodora Ana Mihai’s drama reconstructs the decisions surrounding the 1985 European Cup final at Heysel, where 39 fans died. The review praises its force while noting criticism of its fictionalised details.

image.caption: A scene from Heysel 85.

sources.originalTitle: Heysel 85 review – rage-filled denunciation of the incompetence that fuelled a football disaster

segments.body: Heysel 85 dramatises the 1985 European Cup final between Juventus and Liverpool, where crowd disorder in a poorly maintained, badly policed Brussels stadium led to 39 deaths. The film shows officials allowing the match to proceed, believing that playing it might prevent further disorder.

segments.title: A pointed target
segments.body: The review says the film directs its anger at the complacency of Brussels authorities rather than blaming Liverpool. It also notes criticism of fictionalised elements, including the players’ awareness of the deaths and the portrayal of the city’s mayor, while praising the drama’s immersive intensity.

content.headline: Wicker review – a bawdy fairy tale with a troublingly perfect husband
content.shortHeadline: Wicker is a funny, unsettling fantasy about perfect devotion
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman commissions a husband made of twigs, in a fantasy the review finds hilarious and knowingly sexist. Its comic premise also raises questions about agency, desire and what devotion should mean.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a village outsider who pays a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to create a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s wickerwork figure is devoted to her and eager to please, unsettling a community built around unequal relationships.

segments.title: Fantasy and consent
segments.body: The review enjoys the film’s bawdy humour but questions how little attention it gives the husband’s agency and desires. It argues that the fairy tale’s reversal of familiar gendered expectations can feel like comic score-settling, while cautioning that the fantasy is no model for a real relationship.

content.headline: Young, British and Tradwife review – a provocative look at the movement
content.shortHeadline: Young, British and Tradwife probes a fraught online ideal
content.standfirst: Poppy Jay meets three women with different relationships to tradwife culture, from a mother making online content to a Christian nationalist household. The review welcomes the range but wants tougher questions about money, ambition and influence.

image.caption: Molly with her husband Aaron and their children in Young, British and Tradwife.

sources.originalTitle: Young, British and Tradwife review – TV this frustrating should come with a blood pressure warning

segments.body: Young, British and Tradwife follows three women advocating versions of a lifestyle associated with social media and conservative Christian ideas. The review describes Megan, who earns money through sponsored content featuring her children, Laura Zachary, who posts provocative claims about her marriage, and Molly, a mother of seven whose husband is a Christian nationalist theologian.

segments.title: Questions left open
segments.body: The review praises Jay’s questioning of the men but feels the programme could probe the women’s choices and financial incentives more deeply. It sees the hour as a starting point for harder questions about agency, faith, work and patriarchal expectations—not a definitive account of the movement.

content.headline: I Am Helen shows how toxic masculinity can reshape a relationship
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen brings a woman’s experience of toxic masculinity into focus
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan stars as a woman whose partner ignores her refusal during sex, then struggles to recognise the harm. Two reviews praise the drama’s performances and urgency, while one stresses how it shifts attention to women living with men’s behaviour.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: I Am Helen review – Nicola Coughlan is absolutely superb in this terrifying must-watch
All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: I Am Helen, developed with Nicola Coughlan for Dominic Savage’s anthology, follows Helen and her fiancé Steve after he chokes her during sex despite her saying no. The drama traces the aftermath through their arguments and Steve’s exposure to misogynistic ideas from a colleague, as Helen seeks support and weighs what she wants from her life.

perspectives.body: The i Paper argues that the drama’s force lies in centring the woman affected by toxic masculinity, rather than treating the man’s destructiveness as the main story. It calls the programme vital television, while noting that women have most to gain from its portrayal.

segments.title: A fraught, ordinary aftermath
segments.body: The Guardian review praises Coughlan’s performance and the slow accumulation of threat, while noting that some domestic exchanges feel repetitive. The i Paper also emphasises the unsettling normality of the social attitudes Steve encounters at work and the way his hurt and confusion can turn into anger.

content.headline: The Altruists to Yellowjackets: seven shows to stream this week
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream, from The Altruists to Yellowjackets
content.standfirst: This week’s guide ranges from a drama about cryptocurrency figures Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison to the final season of Yellowjackets. It also picks out comedy, crime, documentary and family viewing.

image.caption: Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists to Yellowjackets: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The week’s recommendations include Netflix’s The Altruists, about FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and his colleague Caroline Ellison, and the fourth and final season of Yellowjackets. Other picks include Belfast-set comedy-drama Rewarding, the documentary The Hotline and a new season of Percy Jackson.

segments.title: More to watch
segments.body: The guide also highlights The Chosen and the two-part Melania series, while noting that the latter follows a feature-length documentary the writer found dull and cringeworthy. Release dates and platforms are listed for each recommendation.

content.headline: Honey review – a playful Killing Eve prequel with Cold War style
content.shortHeadline: Honey’s East Berlin spy story is stylish, funny and uneven
content.standfirst: Ann Skelly plays a young agent in 1980s East Berlin in a series that relishes espionage kitsch and comic reversals. The review finds it entertaining, though less daring once it settles into familiar thriller rhythms.

image.caption: Ann Skelly, Nate Mann and Jannis Niewöhner in Honey.

sources.originalTitle: Honey review – a hugely entertaining Killing Eve prequel that’s packed with naughty jokes

segments.body: Honey follows young agent Martha, undercover in East Berlin in 1982, where her assignments involve luring men into compromising situations. The review praises Ann Skelly’s confident performance, the period detail and the show’s irreverent treatment of familiar spy-thriller scenes.

segments.title: The promise and the pattern
segments.body: As Martha becomes involved with both a CIA agent and a Stasi investigator, the series shifts toward more conventional comedy-thriller plotting. The review says it remains entertaining but does not sustain the early promise of upending spy conventions; its connection to Killing Eve is largely a matter of character backstory.

content.headline: The Body review – camp Catholic-school drama with a dark streak
content.shortHeadline: The Body mixes teen drama, occult panic and 2004 nostalgia
content.standfirst: A Halloween party at an abandoned convent sets off a mystery at a Catholic school in this Netflix drama. The review praises its camp, queer-centred take on teenage desire and shame, though finds the eight episodes could be tighter.

image.caption: The young cast of The Body.

sources.originalTitle: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals

segments.body: Set in 2004, The Body follows a group of Catholic-school girls after an ecstasy-fuelled initiation ritual leaves one student comatose and others experiencing hallucinations and seizures. The review sees the series as a knowingly camp high-school drama, drawing on early-2000s teen films as it explores friendship, desire and social status.

segments.title: Teenage torment
segments.body: The review praises the young cast and the way the series links adolescence to religion: both can be all-consuming and dangerous. It also enjoys the period details, while saying the eight episodes are sluggish and the boys on the sidelines are less compelling than the girls.

content.headline: Keepsake County review – a stealing simulator with a social conscience
content.shortHeadline: Keepsake County finds melancholy in a life of petty theft
content.standfirst: This stealth game sends debt-ridden burglar Samuel through Midwestern McMansions for whatever he can carry. Its repetitive routines become part of a bleak portrait of economic desperation, softened by flashes of delinquent charm.

image.caption: A scene from Keepsake County.

sources.originalTitle: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

segments.body: In Keepsake County, players control Samuel, a burglar who slips into large suburban homes to steal whatever he can sell. The game borrows from extraction shooters but focuses on stealth rather than killing: players pick locks, avoid residents and take their haul to a pawn shop.

segments.title: Repetition and desperation
segments.body: As Samuel’s debt and medical bills emerge, the review finds the break-ins increasingly sad, framing theft as a response to a hopeless financial situation. Repeated dialogue and similar-feeling locations can make play monotonous, but the game’s absurd humour and small acts of petty theft give its bleak setting a delinquent spark.

content.headline: GTA VI hands-on: Rockstar’s vast new world asks players to care
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s new world pairs criminal freedom with a relationship
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s first new Grand Theft Auto in 13 years takes players to fictional Florida with a criminal couple, Lucia and Jason. A hands-on preview finds a more detailed world and new incentives to play with care, as well as the series’ familiar crime.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI

segments.body: In Grand Theft Auto VI, players follow Lucia and Jason through Vice City and the wider fictional state of Leonida. The Guardian’s hands-on preview describes a densely detailed world and a new relationship mechanic: players can nurture the couple’s bond or neglect it, with consequences for their story.

segments.title: Crime with consequences
segments.body: The preview says the game still invites criminal play but encourages players to plan jobs, avoid unnecessary violence and act in character. Rockstar co-head Rob Nelson says the developers wanted to make room for empathy without removing the freedom associated with the series. The game is scheduled for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November.

content.headline: GTA VI’s launch hype obscures questions about worker dismissals
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI hype and sick-day claims distract from a labour dispute
content.standfirst: Reports of mass absences and a billion-dollar productivity hit rest on uncertain or limited estimates, the Guardian finds. Meanwhile, a tribunal case brought by 34 dismissed Rockstar staff is approaching its closing submissions.

image.caption: Former Rockstar developer Will Mesilane, who worked on GTA VI for two years.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?

segments.body: Claims that GTA VI will cause a huge wave of absences and a $1bn US productivity loss have spread widely, but the figures rely on speculative calculations, surveys or limited workforce data. Researchers say some people are likely to take leave for a release this large, but the scale of any economic impact is hard to establish.

segments.title: The dispute behind the launch
segments.body: The article also reports on 34 Rockstar employees dismissed in the UK and Canada, who say they were fired for union activity. Rockstar alleged confidential information was leaked; the company declined to comment for the story. Will Mesilane, one of the dismissed developers, says losing his job forced him and his partner to leave the UK. Closing submissions in the Glasgow tribunal case were scheduled for 17 and 18 November.

content.headline: Game makers turn political satire against Trump’s video game propaganda
content.shortHeadline: Satirical games push back against Trump’s political messaging
content.standfirst: Independent artists and developers are making games that parody the White House’s use of familiar video-game formats for political messaging. Their projects turn the medium into a way to question what those simplified games leave out.

image.caption: The Secret Handshake’s satirical game Operation Epic Furious.

sources.originalTitle: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

segments.body: After the White House launched an online arcade of games promoting its policies, artists and developers created satirical alternatives. The Secret Handshake’s Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell casts players as Donald Trump choosing whether to order a Diet Coke or invade Iran; the group says more than 350,000 people have played its games online.

segments.title: Turning the format around
segments.body: Other projects include Tax Evaders, Corrupt Invaders and Diesel Kong, which use familiar arcade mechanics to criticise political decisions and the cost of living. Their creators say the accessible form lets players experience political headlines differently; one developer describes the White House’s approach as “gamified propaganda”.

content.headline: Elden Ring film faces the challenge of making its world matter on screen
content.shortHeadline: Can an Elden Ring film make its vast world a compelling story?
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation of the hit fantasy game is reportedly in post-production, with a budget said to approach $200m. The central challenge, the article argues, is giving audiences a reason to care about a world as brutal and strange as the game’s.

image.caption: A scene from Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland has reportedly completed filming an Elden Ring adaptation, with Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw, Nick Offerman and others in the cast. The game has sold more than 30 million copies; reported estimates put the film’s budget close to $200m, though the article notes that this figure has not been confirmed.

segments.title: A world needs a story
segments.body: The article points to past fantasy adaptations that struggled to turn elaborate source material into compelling films. Elden Ring’s world leans toward horror, its characters are often dead or grotesque, and the story details remain unknown. The suggestion that the film may draw on events before the game is based on leaked images, not a confirmed account of its plot.

content.headline: AI helps decode Gödel’s notebooks, but historians must judge the result
content.shortHeadline: AI helps uncover Gödel’s hidden mathematical work
content.standfirst: A Finnish logician says Claude helped him digest 1,009 pages of Kurt Gödel’s shorthand notebooks, uncovering hundreds of theorems. Some results have been checked with proof software, but the historical claims still need scrutiny.

image.caption: Kurt Gödel’s unpublished notebooks contain densely written mathematical work.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

segments.body: Jan von Plato, who has spent years studying 16 notebooks by the logician Kurt Gödel, says an AI model helped him make rapid progress through 1,009 densely written pages. Gödel’s notes, much of them in an obsolete German shorthand, contain hundreds of theorems and ideas that von Plato says have not been recognised before.

segments.title: Checking the claims
segments.body: Von Plato says Claude produced a lengthy explanation that he checked page by page. Of 663 theorems and possible theorems identified in the notebooks, he reports that about 400 were verified as stated using the proof assistant Coq, about 200 needed repair and about 50 were false. He also says a reconstructed proof related to the axiom of choice passed Coq.

The historical interpretation remains unsettled. Logician Joel David Hamkins, who has not seen Claude’s reconstruction, says that if it holds up it would be remarkable, but cautions that historians must determine how much belongs to Claude’s reconstruction and how much to Gödel. The source reports von Plato’s findings; it does not establish that all the newly identified work has been independently assessed.

content.headline: Hundreds of children in England prescribed weight-loss drugs, figures show
content.shortHeadline: Hundreds of children prescribed weight-loss drugs in England
content.standfirst: An investigation found 419 children under 18 received GLP-1 prescriptions in England in 2025–26, including 10 under 12. The figures are incomplete, and experts stress the need for specialist care and long-term monitoring.

image.caption: A child receives an injection of a weight-loss medicine.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of children in England prescribed weight-loss jabs, figures show

segments.body: A Guardian investigation found that 419 children under 18 received prescriptions for GLP-1 medicines in the 2025–26 financial year, including 10 children younger than 12. In the four months to July this year, 341 children received prescriptions, 15 of them under 12. The figures cover community prescriptions dispensed in England, but exclude private prescriptions and those dispensed in hospitals or prisons, so they are likely to undercount use.

segments.title: Specialist support matters
segments.body: Experts say these medicines should be used by children within specialist services, with monitoring of growth, puberty, nutrition, mental health, eating behaviours and side effects. Professor Martin Whyte of the University of Surrey also notes that weight can return after treatment stops and that evidence on use over many years in growing children remains limited.

The report describes use for children with severe obesity, sometimes after other support has not helped. NHS specialist services have offered the drugs to some young people, while the World Health Organization’s recent guidance says obesity medicines, including GLP-1s, should not be given to children under 10. The figures do not show whether every prescription was primarily for weight loss.

content.headline: Smartwatch alerts can flag atrial fibrillation, but cannot diagnose it
content.shortHeadline: What smartwatch alerts can—and can’t—tell you about AFib
content.standfirst: Atrial fibrillation can raise the risk of stroke and dementia, and wearable alerts may prompt people to seek help. But a watch cannot diagnose the condition, and alerts can also lead to worry and follow-up testing.

image.caption: A person checks their pulse to look for an irregular heartbeat.

sources.originalTitle: The overlooked sign you could develop dementia – and how your watch could spot it

segments.body: Atrial fibrillation, or AFib, is an irregular heart rhythm that can allow clots to form and increase the risk of stroke. It may also contribute to vascular dementia. Many people do not know they have it: the article estimates that about 1.5 million people in the UK have a diagnosis, with another half a million thought to be undiagnosed.

segments.title: What a watch can show
segments.body: Some smartwatches can alert users to a possible rhythm abnormality, but the devices are not accurate enough to provide a diagnosis. The article describes Heather Armstrong, who sought medical help after her Apple Watch raised an alert; hospital monitoring confirmed AFib. A suspected irregularity still needs medical assessment.

segments.title: The limits of screening
segments.body: A Cambridge researcher quoted in the article warns that a watch may detect a brief episode with no known clinical impact, potentially causing anxiety and extra investigations. A large trial of home heart-rhythm checks in people over 70 is assessing whether detecting and treating AFib reduces strokes, heart disease or dementia; results are expected in 2028.

content.headline: Why a bird-flu outbreak on a Utah mink farm has scientists concerned
content.shortHeadline: Mink farm bird flu raises concern about mutation risk
content.standfirst: Scientists quoted by the i Paper warn that an outbreak among mink could create opportunities for bird flu to change or mix with seasonal flu. The article describes a potential risk, not evidence that the virus is spreading between people.

image.caption: Mink on a fur farm, the type of animal at the centre of the reported bird-flu concerns.

sources.originalTitle: Bird flu is one mutation from serious risk to humans – how prepared is the UK?

segments.body: An outbreak of bird flu among mink on a Utah fur farm has raised concern among scientists because the animals’ respiratory systems resemble those of humans. The i Paper reports that the outbreak had been under way since at least August. The virus has occasionally infected people working with animals, but the article says it has not been shown to spread easily from person to person.

segments.title: A risk, not a prediction
segments.body: Experts quoted in the report say mink could provide conditions for the virus to change, or for bird and seasonal flu viruses to exchange genetic material if both circulate in an animal or a worker. The article describes these as risks; it does not report that such a change has occurred or that the outbreak has led to human-to-human transmission.

segments.title: Preparedness questions
segments.body: The report also highlights gaps experts want tested, including whether existing flu tests can identify bird flu and how quickly a suitable test could be developed. One expert calls for a practical exercise to produce a bird-flu lateral-flow test, rather than relying only on planning exercises. The article notes that a new vaccine made with standard methods could take six months, while an mRNA approach might be faster.

content.headline: NHS in England to keep Palantir data contract until 2029
content.shortHeadline: Palantir’s NHS data contract extended to 2029
content.standfirst: Ministers will let Palantir’s £330m NHS data contract run until 2029 while preparing a procurement process for British suppliers. Critics say the wait is too long; questions about trust and the platform’s use remain.

image.caption: Campaigners protest outside Bristol Royal Infirmary over NHS England’s data contract with Palantir.

sources.originalTitle: NHS data contract to stay with Palantir until 2029
Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

segments.body: The government will keep Palantir’s contract to provide England’s NHS federated data platform until 2029, rather than use a break clause to end it earlier. The £330m arrangement, intended to help link healthcare providers and manage hospital waiting lists, was due to run until 2031. Ministers say the extension gives them time to invite British companies to bid to replace the US firm.

segments.title: Dispute over trust and use
segments.body: Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs, the British Medical Association and campaign groups have criticised the delay. The Guardian reports that many NHS trusts have declined to use the platform and that 29 trusts were using it never or rarely, prompting NHS England to remove a claim about 137 trusts benefiting from it. The government says a replacement process must maintain public trust and clinical confidence.

Palantir says the programme is exceeding targets and has helped deliver more operations, speed up hospital discharge and reduce waits for cancer diagnoses. Critics have also raised concerns about patient-data use and the company’s other government and military work. The BBC reports the government plans to begin procurement next summer.

perspectives.body: Palantir says its NHS work is exceeding targets, citing more operations, faster discharge and shorter waits for patients awaiting cancer diagnoses.

content.headline: Microsoft says months-old bug contributed to global services outage
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft traces global outage to bug, network failure and capacity
content.standfirst: Microsoft says a latent software bug, a failed network gateway and reduced server capacity combined to cause a 24-hour disruption to Outlook, Exchange and other services. The company says a fuller report is still to come.

image.caption: Microsoft signage outside an office building in New York.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
Everything we know about the Microsoft outage as Outlook and Teams come back online

segments.body: Microsoft has identified three factors behind last week’s outage of Outlook, Exchange and other services: a bug dating back to July, a network gateway problem and reduced server capacity. The company says the combination caused requests to build up until servers stopped responding during a peak period of US traffic.

segments.title: Why recovery took time
segments.body: Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said one of the company’s two network gateways was not working for Teams, increasing load on the other, while more than 14% of server capacity was unavailable because of an unrelated issue. Recovery was slow because returning servers were overwhelmed by waiting traffic, and ordinary rollback tools could not quickly remove a bug introduced months earlier.

The outage disrupted email and other services used by organisations around the world. The i Paper’s earlier account described schools, hospitals, businesses and public services struggling to communicate during the disruption. Microsoft said the incident was not caused by a cybersecurity breach and plans to publish a final report with more detail.

content.headline: Uber and Zipline begin commercial drone food deliveries in Texas
content.shortHeadline: Uber Eats starts drone food deliveries in Texas
content.standfirst: Customers in Spring, near Houston, can order food delivered by Zipline drones, with Dallas next in the companies’ plans. Their goal of one million daily deliveries by 2029 is ambitious; the industry remains early and faces community concerns.

sources.originalTitle: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow
Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston

segments.body: Uber Eats and Zipline have begun commercial drone food deliveries in Spring, Texas, the first launch under their partnership. Customers in the service area can select participating restaurants in the app; the aircraft carry orders weighing up to eight pounds and lower them to a delivery spot in a protective pod on a tether rather than landing.

segments.title: Expansion plans and constraints
segments.body: The companies plan to expand to Dallas and other US cities, with a target of one million deliveries a day by the end of 2029. The Verge reports that Zipline currently averages about 4,300 deliveries a day worldwide, putting the scale of that goal in context. Residents in some communities have raised concerns about drone noise, wildlife, safety and privacy.

perspectives.body: The Verge notes the gap between the companies’ one-million-a-day ambition and Zipline’s reported current average of roughly 4,300 deliveries a day worldwide.

segments.body: Zipline says its aircraft fly above 300 feet and can travel at up to 70 miles per hour. The company’s US expansion followed Federal Aviation Administration certification in 2022. The reporting describes a nascent service and does not establish how quickly customers or communities will adopt it at scale.

content.headline: Microsoft says Windows 11 now works better on laptops with 8GB of RAM
content.shortHeadline: Windows 11 runs better on 8GB of RAM, but has limits
content.standfirst: A Verge retest found fewer slowdowns after Microsoft changed memory management in Windows 11. The improvement makes 8GB machines more usable under load, but the reviewer still recommends 16GB where possible.

sources.originalTitle: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

segments.body: A Verge reviewer retested a Microsoft Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM after installing a newer Windows 11 build. Compared with the earlier version, the laptop handled more open browser tabs, video streaming and chat apps with fewer slowdowns and less frequent page reloads. The reviewer also observed fewer memory-related hard faults during the test.

segments.title: Still a compromise
segments.body: Microsoft says its lab tests found Windows up to 20% more responsive and multitasking up to 40% faster.
